body.title: Why We Publish Market Notes
body.content:
Penn Jets publishes short notes on the private aviation market because the questions we are asked most often deserve a better answer than a phone call can give.

Buyers and sellers are usually working with incomplete information. Aircraft transactions are private by nature, comparable sales are rarely published, and the figures that do circulate are often months out of date by the time they reach anyone making a decision. That gap is where bad assumptions form.

What we write here comes out of transactions we have actually worked on and aircraft we have actually inspected. When we describe how a model is holding value, or why a particular segment has tightened, it reflects what we are seeing in the market rather than what is convenient to say.

We publish these notes for the same reason we take the time to walk a client through a pre-buy inspection report line by line: an informed counterparty makes for a cleaner transaction. If something here raises a question about your own aircraft or a purchase you are considering, we would rather you asked.

body.title: The Light Jet Market in 2026: Why Smaller Business Jets Could Lead the Next Decade
body.content:
The private jet market continues to evolve in 2026, and some of the most interesting activity is occurring well below the ultra-long-range category.

Light jets remain the most actively traded portion of the pre-owned business jet market, while long-term forecasts point toward substantial growth in both light jets and very light jets (VLJs). For buyers, sellers, and aircraft owners, the underlying question is simple: why are smaller business jets attracting so much attention?

Part of the answer comes down to mission. Many private aviation trips simply do not require an aircraft capable of flying halfway around the world.

A Market Positioned for Long-Term Growth

A September 2026 market forecast reported by Aviation International News estimates that the overall business jet market could grow from approximately $27 billion in 2025 to more than $60.5 billion annually by 2035.

The forecast is particularly notable at the smaller end of business aviation. Market research projects the light-jet segment growing from approximately $4.44 billion in 2025 to $16.47 billion by 2035. The VLJ segment is projected to grow from approximately $1.31 billion to $6.3 billion over the same period.

Those projections should not be interpreted as guaranteed future aircraft values. They do, however, illustrate expectations for significant investment and demand within aircraft categories sometimes overshadowed by large-cabin jets.

Why the Mission Matters

Range receives enormous attention when aircraft are marketed, but maximum range and actual mission requirements are very different things.

According to the same market research, flights below 500 nautical miles accounted for approximately 58.3% of global business jet activity in 2025.

For missions like New York to Washington, Miami to the Bahamas, Dallas to Houston, or Los Angeles to Las Vegas, an owner may gain relatively little practical benefit from carrying the acquisition and operating costs of substantially more aircraft than the mission requires.

This is where light jets become compelling. Aircraft such as the Embraer Phenom 300, Citation CJ family, Citation M2, and HondaJet combine speed and business-jet capability with operating economics designed around regional travel.

Small Jets Remain the Most Actively Traded

Current pre-owned transaction data reinforces the importance of this category.

JETNET reported 544 Small Jet transactions during the first half of 2026, making them the most actively traded cabin class. Transactions were down 9.6% compared with an unusually active first half of 2025, but Small Jets still accounted for nearly half of the 1,115 pre-owned business jet transactions recorded during the period.

More recent JETNET data through July showed Small Jets remaining the most actively traded class, with 1,342 transactions on a trailing-twelve-month basis.

Liquidity matters when purchasing an aircraft. A larger installed fleet, active transaction market, established maintenance network, and broad buyer population can become important advantages when it is eventually time to sell.

Inventory Is Tight—Especially for Younger Aircraft

The market becomes even more interesting when inventory is considered.

JETNET reported that aircraft available for sale represented approximately 6.6% of the operational business jet fleet in mid-2026, down from 7.3% in 2025 and considerably below the 9% to 12% levels common during much of the decade before the pandemic.

But not all inventory is equal.

Approximately 74% of business jets currently offered for sale are 16 years old or older. The newest aircraft represent only a small portion of available inventory.

Global Jet Capital similarly reported that only 3.7% of the fleet aged 12 years or younger was available for sale at the end of Q2 2026.

That creates two different markets: buyers seeking late-model aircraft face limited supply, while buyers willing to consider older airframes generally have more options and potentially greater negotiating leverage.

Pricing Is Becoming More Rational

The extraordinary pricing environment of 2021 through 2023 has continued to normalize.

JETNET's July market report placed the trailing-twelve-month average asking price for Small Jets at approximately $3.52 million. While individual aircraft values vary dramatically, Small Jet pricing remains substantially above 2019 levels.

Global Jet Capital also found that values for aircraft 12 years old and younger increased 3.3% during Q2 2026, compared with a 1.9% increase among aircraft 13 years and older.

For buyers, this reinforces the importance of looking beyond the asking price. Two aircraft of the same model year can have substantially different economic values depending on engine program status, maintenance history, inspection timing, total time, avionics, interior condition, damage history, and pedigree.

Newer Aircraft Are Selling Faster

Aircraft age is also having a measurable effect on liquidity.

JETNET reports that business jets between zero and five years old are selling in approximately 53 days, while every age category 16 years and older is averaging more than 100 days on market.

For a seller with a late-model, well-maintained light jet, that scarcity can create leverage. For someone selling an older aircraft, accurate pricing and a clear understanding of upcoming maintenance become increasingly important.

Fractional Growth Matters to the Light-Jet Market

Another important development is the continued expansion of fractional aviation.

JETNET reports that fractional program operators accounted for approximately 18% of new business jet deliveries through 2026, compared with roughly 10% before the pandemic.

Fractional and shared-access models naturally favor aircraft that can fly frequently and efficiently. That does not benefit every light-jet model equally, but it reinforces demand for aircraft offering strong dispatch reliability, reasonable direct operating costs, and useful cabin capability.

What Buyers Should Watch

The light-jet market offers opportunity, but buyers should resist treating every aircraft in the category as interchangeable.

  • Mission: Buy for the trips you actually fly, not the longest trip you might take once.
  • Maintenance: Understand upcoming inspections, engine exposure, and program coverage.
  • Inventory: Late-model aircraft remain scarce, so exceptional examples can move quickly.
  • Fleet support: Consider parts availability, service centers, and installed fleet size.
  • Exit strategy: Think about resale before purchasing, particularly with older aircraft.

What Sellers Should Watch

For sellers, the market remains selective rather than universally strong.

A late-model aircraft with complete records, strong maintenance status, desirable avionics, and program-covered engines occupies a very different market position from an older aircraft approaching expensive inspections.

Pricing should therefore be based on comparable aircraft and recent transactions—not simply what another owner is asking online.

The Next Decade of Light Aviation

The long-term forecasts are significant, but the more important story may be what is already happening.

Business jet utilization remains above pre-pandemic levels. Inventory remains historically tight. Younger aircraft are scarce. Fractional operators continue taking a larger share of new deliveries, and Small Jets remain the most actively traded class in the pre-owned market.

For many owners, the future of private aviation may not mean flying farther. It may mean selecting an aircraft more precisely matched to the mission.

That combination of accessibility, efficiency, airport flexibility, and active resale demand is why the light-jet market deserves close attention as private aviation enters its next decade of growth.

Final Approach

The best aircraft is not necessarily the largest, newest, or longest-range airplane available. It is the aircraft that consistently accomplishes the owner's mission while making economic and operational sense.

In 2026, the light-jet market is demonstrating exactly why that distinction matters.

Written by Joseph Pennella
Penn Jets LLC

body.title: Pilatus PC-12 NGX: A Modern Look at the Most Capable Turboprop in the Sky
body.content:
Introduction

Few aircraft have reshaped private aviation like the Pilatus PC-12. The NGX variant advances that reputation by combining the rugged utility of earlier models with the sophistication typically seen only in light jets. Owners choose the NGX for its combination of speed, fuel efficiency, and short-field credentials — but the real story lies in the technology behind it.

1. Powerplant Evolution: Smarter, Faster, More Efficient

The NGX features the Pratt & Whitney PT6E-67XP, the first engine in the PC-12 family to integrate digital engine control.
Key advantages:

FADEC-equivalent control allows simplified power management — one lever, fewer pilot workload steps.

Automatic start sequencing reduces risk of hot starts.

Optimized fuel flow improves cruise speeds by roughly 3–5% compared to prior generations.

Extended TBO options support lower long-term DOCs for high-utilization operators.

This level of automation is rare in turboprops and is a major contributor to the NGX’s modern handling.

2. Avionics: A Jet-Class Flight Deck in a Turboprop Airframe

The NGX uses an advanced version of the Honeywell Apex integrated cockpit. While not identical to jet platforms like the G3000/G5000, the software logic and display philosophy lean heavily into jet-level situational awareness.

Highlights include:

Cursor Control Device (CCD) for intuitive flight management

SmartView synthetic vision

Advanced envelope protection to reduce unintended stalls or overspeed events

IFIS features including charts, graphical weather, and airport diagrams

Integrated autopilot with improved vertical navigation logic

The result is a workload environment closer to a light jet than a traditional turboprop.

3. Cabin: Quiet, Pressurized, and Configurable for Every Mission

The NGX introduced a more refined interior with:

Larger windows for improved natural lighting

Quieter cabin acoustics thanks to propeller and power management improvements

New seat architecture modeled after the PC-24

Multiple layouts ranging from executive seating to mixed cargo configurations

For owners needing a do-everything aircraft — corporate missions, medical transport, or rough-field landings — the NGX cabin is a key differentiator.

4. Propeller & Performance Enhancements

Pilatus partnered with Hartzell to optimize propeller and blade geometry, resulting in:

Reduced cabin noise

Improved low-speed control on short runways

Faster climb performance

Selectable prop speeds to tailor noise profile vs. performance

Combined with robust landing gear and Pilatus’s STOL-friendly wing, the NGX remains one of the most capable unimproved runway performers in the industry.

5. Safety Architecture: Redundancy by Design

While the PC-12 is a single-engine platform, its safety record and engineering approach are often compared to twin-engine turboprops.

Its safety ecosystem includes:

Dual electrical buses and backup power pathways

Redundant flight-critical sensors

Automated engine protection logic

Powerful pressurization and environmental systems

Exceptional glide ratio due to efficient wing design

This combination is why operators trust the PC-12 worldwide in environments ranging from high-altitude strips to commercial shuttle networks.

6. Mission Economics & Why Owners Choose It

The PC-12 NGX is widely considered one of the most cost-effective aircraft in its class.

Typical operating cost advantages:

Turboprop fuel efficiency

Simplified engine management reduces wear

Long TBO and favorable maintenance intervals

Versatile commercial use under Part 135

Ability to operate from inexpensive secondary airports

For many owners, the NGX replaces both a cabin-class piston and a light jet — covering 90% of their missions with significantly lower hourly cost.

7. Who the NGX Is Perfect For

Owners who benefit most from the PC-12 NGX typically have:

Frequent regional missions of 200–900 nm

Need for short, narrow, or unpaved runway access

Flexible missions: family travel, corporate trips, cargo capability

Interest in lower DOCs without sacrificing comfort

Desire for a single-pilot certified aircraft with jet-like avionics

The NGX remains one of the few aircraft that can fly executives to a major city, land on a mountain strip, and then convert to cargo hauling — all in the same day

Conclusion

The Pilatus PC-12 NGX is more than an upgraded turboprop — it’s a technology platform designed to merge efficiency with capability. With advanced engine automation, a sophisticated cockpit, and unmatched versatility, the NGX continues to set the standard for owners who want performance without the operating costs of a jet. In the 2025 market, it remains one of the most compelling aircraft in its class.

body.title: September 11 and the Evolution of Private Aviation
body.content:
September 11, 2001, changed aviation forever.

Before discussing what those changes meant for private aviation, aircraft ownership, fractional programs, and charter, it is important first to remember the nearly 3,000 people who lost their lives, the first responders who answered the call, and the families and communities whose lives were forever changed.

The effects of September 11 extended throughout aviation. The United States entered an entirely new security environment, and both commercial and general aviation were required to adapt to new procedures, restrictions, regulations, and expectations.

Private aviation changed as well.

A Changing Relationship With Private Aviation

Flying privately means something different to every individual who uses it. Some pilots own and fly their own aircraft. Some individuals own an aircraft outright and rely on a professional crew or management company. Others participate through fractional ownership, while many use charter for intermittent travel or immediate transportation needs.

In the period following September 11, travelers began looking at these options differently.

A 2002 report from the University of California, Berkeley’s Institute of Transportation Studies cited an Air Charter Guide survey that found demand for air charter services increased approximately 30% following September 11. The report also stated that 84% of respondents continued to experience increased inquiries after October 2001 and noted increased activity among fractional aviation operators.

Those numbers represented more than simply an increase in demand. They reflected a changing relationship between travelers and aviation.

Private aviation had always offered flexibility, efficiency, and access. Following September 11, the ability to exercise greater control over an itinerary, choose airports closer to a destination, establish relationships with trusted operators, and reduce dependence on large commercial terminals became increasingly meaningful to many travelers and businesses.

Aviation Adapts

At the same time, general aviation itself faced substantial changes and restrictions. Aviation security became an even greater national priority, and the regulatory environment continued to evolve.

Today, the FAA maintains an extensive framework governing aircraft operations, pilot qualifications, maintenance, commercial operators, and aviation safety. Security procedures and operating standards throughout the aviation industry have continued to develop during the twenty-five years since September 11.

But one of the most important aspects of private aviation cannot necessarily be measured by regulation, aircraft performance, or flight time.

It is trust.

The Value of Trust and Continuity

There is tremendous value in having a routine you trust and people you trust.

body.title: Bombardier, U.S. Market Access and What Trump’s Latest Restrictions Could Mean for Private Aviation
body.content:
Private aviation has been pulled into the latest chapter of the U.S.-Canada trade dispute. In September 2026, President Donald Trump threatened to prevent Bombardier from selling aircraft in the United States unless the Canadian manufacturer builds its aircraft in America.

For business aviation, this is more than a political headline. Bombardier is one of the world’s leading business-jet manufacturers, and the United States is an important market for its Challenger and Global families. If meaningful restrictions are implemented, the effects could reach new-aircraft availability, pre-owned values, purchasing decisions, and competition across the super-midsize and large-cabin markets.

What Has Actually Happened?

The distinction between a proposed restriction and an enacted restriction is important. Trump has publicly stated that Bombardier should not be permitted to sell aircraft in the United States unless it manufactures them domestically. Exactly how such a restriction would be implemented, and which aircraft or transactions would be affected, remains unclear.

This follows an earlier dispute in January 2026, when Trump threatened a 50% tariff on Canadian-built aircraft and potential decertification of Canadian aircraft amid a disagreement involving Canada’s certification of Gulfstream aircraft. Those broader threats did not ultimately take effect as originally described.

Buyers and sellers should therefore treat the current situation as a developing market risk rather than assume Bombardier aircraft have suddenly become unusable or unmarketable in the United States.

Why Bombardier Matters

Bombardier occupies an important position in private aviation. The Challenger family competes heavily in the super-midsize and large-cabin markets, while the Global series competes at the highest end of business aviation against Gulfstream and Dassault.

Aircraft including the Challenger 3500, Challenger 650, Global 6500, and Global 7500 are established platforms for private owners, corporate flight departments, and charter operators.

Bombardier also has an extensive U.S. economic footprint through American suppliers, service operations, facilities, and employees. The situation is therefore more complicated than simply treating Bombardier as a foreign manufacturer.

What Could Happen to New Bombardier Aircraft?

The most immediate exposure would likely involve new-aircraft transactions. If tariffs, import restrictions, or another mechanism limiting Bombardier deliveries are implemented, U.S. buyers could face higher acquisition costs or reduced availability.

The outcome depends on the final policy. A tariff would create a very different market response from an outright sales prohibition or certification restriction.

Anyone currently negotiating a new Challenger or Global purchase should pay particular attention to contract provisions involving tariffs, taxes, delivery location, import requirements, regulatory changes, and termination rights.

The Pre-Owned Market Could Be the Bigger Story

If restrictions primarily affect newly manufactured aircraft entering the United States, existing U.S.-based Bombardier aircraft could become increasingly attractive.

A buyer who planned to order a new Challenger might instead pursue a late-model aircraft already operating domestically. If enough buyers make that decision, available pre-owned inventory could tighten.

That does not guarantee higher values. Aircraft pricing still depends on age, total time, maintenance status, engine programs, pedigree, configuration, damage history, and market demand. But restricting new supply could create additional demand for desirable late-model Challengers and Globals.

Could Gulfstream Benefit?

Bombardier and Gulfstream compete aggressively for many of the same customers. Any prolonged limitation on Bombardier’s access to U.S. buyers could redirect some demand toward American-built Gulfstream aircraft.

However, these aircraft are not interchangeable. Buyers evaluate range, cabin dimensions, runway performance, operating economics, acquisition price, delivery availability, and personal preference.

Another consideration is production capacity. If demand shifts toward competing manufacturers, delivery positions could tighten, potentially supporting both new-aircraft pricing and late-model pre-owned values across competing platforms.

What Existing Bombardier Owners Should Watch

Existing owners should avoid reacting to headlines alone. Restricting future imports is fundamentally different from affecting aircraft already registered and operating in the United States.

Instead, owners should monitor:

  • Comparable U.S. inventory
  • Average days on market
  • Transaction volume and pricing
  • New-aircraft delivery availability
  • Financing and insurance appetite
  • FAA or federal regulatory actions

These indicators will provide a clearer picture of actual aircraft values than political statements by themselves.

What Buyers Should Do

Prospective buyers should separate the quality of the aircraft from the uncertainty surrounding trade policy. Challenger and Global aircraft have not fundamentally changed because of a political dispute.

For new aircraft, agreements should clearly address tariffs, import restrictions, delivery requirements, and regulatory contingencies. For pre-owned aircraft, buyers should carefully verify title, registration, location, maintenance status, and import history.

Most importantly, a multimillion-dollar aircraft decision should not be based solely on speculation about what Washington or Ottawa may do next.

What Sellers Should Watch

For sellers, the situation could become either an opportunity or a headwind. If new supply is restricted while existing aircraft remain freely transferable, high-quality U.S.-based Challengers and Globals could become more desirable.

If regulatory uncertainty instead concerns buyers, financing sources, or future resale prospects, the market could demand additional discounts. The direction will depend on what policy is actually implemented.

The Bigger Picture

The Bombardier situation demonstrates that aircraft values are influenced by more than flight hours, maintenance status, and market inventory. Trade policy, certification, manufacturing origin, and geopolitical risk can also affect multimillion-dollar aviation assets.

For buyers and sellers, the lesson is simple: evaluate the aircraft and the environment surrounding the aircraft.

Final Approach

Trump’s latest statements introduce uncertainty into one of private aviation’s most competitive markets, but uncertainty should not be confused with completed policy.

If restrictions ultimately take effect, the consequences could extend beyond Bombardier—potentially influencing pre-owned Challenger and Global values, Gulfstream demand, factory delivery positions, and acquisition strategies throughout the U.S. business-jet market.

Penn Jets will continue watching inventory, transaction activity, and regulatory developments as the market responds.

Written by Joseph Pennella
Penn Jets LLC

body.content:
Quickstart: 10 Steps to Your First Jet

1. Define the Mission
Pax count, range, runways, weather, baggage, cabin needs, international profile.
Ranges:

300–800 nm (VLJ/Light)

1,000–1,800 nm (Light/Super-Light)

1,800–2,400 nm (Midsize)

2,400–3,200 nm (Super-Mid)

3,500+ nm (Large/ULR)
Consider short/high/contaminated runways, Wi-Fi class, lav type, and ops hours (200 Part 91 vs 500+ with charter).

2. Fix the Budget
Set purchase cap + 12-month operating budget with 10–15% contingency.
One-time: escrow/title/legal $15k–$45k; sales/use tax varies; pre-buy $12k–$80k; upgrades $25k–$400k.
Annual fixed: mgmt $60k–$180k; crew $240k–$750k; hangar/insurance $60k–$220k.
Variable/hr:

Light: $1,800–$3,200

Mid/Super-Mid: $3,200–$5,200

Large: $5,500–$9,500+

3. Choose Ownership Model

Sole (Part 91): max control, higher fixeds.

Co-own/Fractional: shared capex + scheduling.

Dry Lease-Back: flexible with correct legal structure.

Charter-Managed (135): 250–500 revenue hrs/yr possible; offsets costs but adds cycles.
Set target use (ex: 200 owner + 300 charter hours).

4. Financing Essentials
Asset-based loans 5–10 yrs, 15–20 yr amortization; 60–85% LTV. Leases (TRAC/finance lease) for flexibility.
Lenders want: liquidity (6–24 months debt service), net worth, strong income, aircraft marketability.
Speed closing by preparing: 3 yrs financials, PFS, business overview, management plan.

5. Tax & Legal
Use a single-purpose aircraft LLC.
Plan delivery state to manage sales/use tax.
Bonus depreciation phases down (≈40% in 2025). Requires qualified business use.
Track any personal use.
Keep Part 91 vs 135 operations clean.
International ops may require eAPIS, cabotage compliance, OFAC/Sanctions, ETS/CORSIA.

6. Insurance Reality
Typical limits: $50M–$200M CSL.
Premium drivers: pilot total/type time, training, SMS, management company, claims history.
Start early—new owners in older jets can be difficult without pro crews.

7. Technical Due Diligence (Pre-Buy)
Verify logbooks, AD/SB compliance, damage history, CAMP/Traxxall, LLP traceability, RVSM/LPV/FANS.
Independent facility only.
Scope: engines/APU borescopes, hot-section, corrosion, gear cycles, pressurization leaks, avionics/Wi-Fi function.
Programs: MSP/JSSI/Smart Parts—check transfer fees and enrollment gaps.

8. The Deal (LOI → Purchase Agreement → Close)
LOI: price, refundable deposit in escrow, pre-buy facility/scope, acceptance criteria, squawk remedy process, return-to-service standards, title/lien release, right to walk.
Purchase Agreement: warranties, delivery condition, risk of loss, insurance, taxes, governing law.
Closing: FAA filings (8050-1/2), lien releases, IR filings, manuals, spares, keys, data subscriptions, insurance binders.

9. Standing Up Operations (Day 0–30)
Management: compare proposals (fees, crew sourcing, training, MEL control, 24/7 dispatch).
Crew: PIC/SIC type-rated; training booked pre-close.
Maintenance: select MRO; set up CAMP/Traxxall, parts accounts, AOG plan.
Base: hangar with power/tow/security.
Safety: MEL, SMS (recommended even Part 91), emergency plan, LOAs, IS-BAO optional.
Connectivity: verify Wi-Fi transfer; negotiate multi-year plan.

10. Charter Offset (Optional)
Best models: Phenom/CJ series, PC-12, mids/super-mids.
Realistic net: covers 20–60% of fixeds.
More cycles = more maintenance.
Negotiate owner-priority windows + hourly reserve contributions.

Resale & Exit Strategy
Buy mid-life, proven fleets.
Keep logs pristine; avoid deferrals.
Watch comp sales + days-on-market.
Plan major inspections around resale timing.

Red Flags
Missing logs, damage without documentation, corrosion, engines off-program with looming HSI/overhaul, “fix after close,” unrealistic charter promises.

body.content:
Sustainable Aviation: The Future of Private Flying
Exploring eco-friendly alternatives and the innovations shaping tomorrow’s skies

Private aviation has long symbolized freedom, efficiency, and prestige. But as global attention turns toward climate responsibility, the industry faces a defining question: Can luxury flight go green? The answer, increasingly, is yes — thanks to groundbreaking propulsion technologies, sustainable fuels, and bold commitments from major players like NetJets and startups such as Otto Aviation.

The Environmental Reality of Private Jet Travel

Private jets account for less than 0.2% of global aviation emissions — but they emit up to 10 times more carbon per passenger than commercial airliners. As scrutiny grows, particularly in Europe and the U.S., operators, manufacturers, and owners alike are rethinking how to align convenience and conscience.

Sustainability in private aviation now goes far beyond carbon offsets. It’s becoming a strategic pillar across manufacturing, operations, and finance. The State of the Private Jet Market — Q3 2025

An in-depth look at market trends, pricing, and what buyers and sellers can expect next.

A Market That’s Finding Its Rhythm Again

After a bumpy start to the year, the private aviation sector closed out Q3 2025 with renewed energy. Business-jet flight activity surged in September, marking one of the strongest non-COVID monthly increases in nearly a decade. Fractional operators like NetJets, Flexjet, and PlaneSense led the charge, while traditional charter demand remained steady across key U.S. regions and transatlantic routes.

In short, the skies are busy again — but the way people are buying, selling, and flying jets continues to evolve.

OEM Deliveries: Momentum Is Back

Aircraft manufacturers saw a decisive rebound this quarter:

Gulfstream delivered 39 aircraft in Q3, up from 28 last year — its best quarter since the pandemic recovery began.

Textron Aviation matched that pace with 42 Citations handed over to clients, buoyed by a strong pipeline of midsize orders.

Embraer held steady with 41 executive jets, led by continued Phenom 300 demand.

Honeywell’s 10-year forecast now projects 8,500 new business jets worth $283 billion through 2035 — signaling long-term confidence in private aviation’s fundamentals.

Supply chains have largely normalized, and new-jet production is finally catching up to backlog demand. For buyers waiting on new deliveries, 2026–27 slots are already tightening across multiple OEMs.

Pre-Owned Market: Tight, But Rational

The pre-owned segment remains a tale of two markets.
Inventory across the business-jet fleet hovered around 6.5%, still below the 10-year average of 7.6%. Dealers reported rising confidence and willingness to carry inventory, which typically signals a more balanced, sustainable pricing environment.

According to AMSTAT data, total transactions for the first three quarters of 2025 are up 11% year-over-year, with a strong rebound in Q3 offsetting mid-year softness. Mid-size and light jets led the activity, while turboprops cooled slightly.

Pricing: Stable, with a Firm Floor

For younger aircraft (2015 and newer), competition remains intense. Buyers are paying premiums for low-time, well-maintained examples with clean pedigrees and modern avionics.

Older models — especially those facing major maintenance or upgrade events — are trading more slowly and at condition-adjusted values. Sellers who price realistically are moving their aircraft efficiently; those who don’t, risk sitting.

Charter rates remain elevated but steady. According to Avinode, U.S. charter pricing is holding near 2024 highs, with slight regional softening offset by peak-season surcharges.

Buyer’s Outlook: Be Decisive, Be Prepared

Buyers entering Q4 should expect:

Tight supply of late-model light and super-mid jets.

Limited OEM slots for 2026 delivery — lock positions early.

Higher MRO demand — pre-purchase inspection (PPI) scheduling now takes longer than expected.

Tax-driven competition heading into year-end; bonus depreciation and business-use structuring remain top-of-mind.

If you’re serious about acquiring, work closely with your broker, lender, and tax advisor before sending your LOI. Aligning delivery timing with financial planning can save six figures in depreciation benefits.

Seller’s Outlook: Orderly Market, Solid Demand

For sellers, the story is equally encouraging.
Dealer sentiment improved, and average time-on-market shortened for aircraft with complete records and cosmetic freshness. Buyers are still selective — but good airplanes are moving.

Tips for maximizing resale value:

Provide recent borescope and engine-trend data upfront.

Highlight maintenance program enrollment (e.g., MSP, JSSI).

Offer escrow holdbacks or limited warranties for older aircraft to keep deals moving quickly.

Segment Highlights

Light & Midsize Jets: Strongest resale activity; top performers include the Citation XLS+, Phenom 300, and Lear 75.

Large Cabin: OEM deliveries accelerating; Gulfstream G700/G800 and Bombardier Global 8000 orders keep backlogs firm.

Turboprops: Market softening; buyers have leverage unless airframes are low-time or special-mission equipped.

What’s Next

Heading into Q4 and early 2026, all signs point to a stable, confident market. New-jet deliveries are catching up, charter activity remains robust, and fractional programs continue to attract new entrants who value flexibility over ownership overhead.

For serious buyers and sellers, this is a market that rewards preparation and decisiveness — not speculation.

Final Thought

Private aviation remains one of the most resilient corners of the transportation industry. Whether you’re purchasing your first light jet or upgrading to a long-range platform, the fundamentals are strong: steady demand, disciplined supply, and growing confidence among both manufacturers and brokers.

The bottom line: Q3 2025 showed that the jet market is healthy, efficient, and moving with purpose — a sign that luxury aviation is not just back, but maturing into a smarter, more sustainable cycle.

body.title: Jet Charter vs. Ownership: Making the Right Choice
body.content:
The Big Question,

Private aviation gives you freedom and efficiency that commercial travel can’t. But before taking that leap, there’s one question that determines everything: should you own or charter your aircraft?

I’ve seen it firsthand. My father was an avid aviator for many years and an owner-operator himself. Growing up around him and his associates, I’ve seen this debate play out since childhood. Now in my late twenties, working in the aviation world myself, I hear the same conversation between new buyers, legacy operators, and Part 91 flyers. One of my earliest mentors, Steven Smyth, a veteran pilot and the owner of KLM Aviation Inc., a Part 135 operator based in Fort Lauderdale, shared lessons with me that still hold true today.

What I’ve learned is this: the lifecycle of aircraft ownership is rarely what prospective buyers imagine. Many new owners underestimate the ongoing costs, management responsibilities, and operational complexity. Private aviation is expensive, but with the right team behind you, it can also become a cash-flowing investment rather than a financial burden.

In today’s market, you have multiple options: jet cards, charter programs, fractional ownership under Part 91, or shared operations under Part 135. This conversation surfaces across every corner of private aviation, from legacy operators to first-time buyers. So, should you own or charter?

At Penn Jets, we help clients look at both the numbers and the lifestyle behind each choice. Here’s what really matters when deciding how to travel privately.

Understanding the Basics

Ownership means buying an aircraft outright, financing it entirely, or acquiring a share through a fractional program. Ownership gives you control over scheduling, customization, and management, and with the right consulting and management team, it can also provide meaningful tax advantages. Without the right support, your new aircraft can quickly start controlling you instead of the other way around. Both Part 91 (private use) and Part 135 (charter) ownership come with fixed costs including maintenance, crew, insurance, hangar space, and management. The difference lies in their purpose and level of FAA regulatory compliance.

Under Part 135, an aircraft can legally generate charter revenue when operated in full compliance with FAA rules, standards, and oversight. Under Part 91, the operator is limited to private use only, meaning the aircraft cannot carry paying charter clientele. Both structures may still qualify for significant tax benefits, including potential bonus depreciation of up to 100 percent in the first year of ownership. To qualify, the aircraft must generally be used at least 50 percent for business purposes and meet individual financial and tax requirements.

Charter allows you to pay only when you fly. It’s flexible, straightforward, and commitment-free. You can choose aircraft types based on each trip and avoid the long-term responsibilities of ownership, a clean getaway for many travelers.

Cost Overview

When deciding between owning or chartering, the first factor that comes into play is cost. Ownership requires a significant upfront investment, anywhere from around one million dollars for a light jet to well over seventy million for a large cabin aircraft. Fractional ownership programs typically start between two hundred thousand and two million dollars depending on the share size and aircraft type.

Beyond the purchase, owners take on ongoing expenses: fuel, maintenance, insurance, hangar fees, crew salaries, and management oversight. These costs are fixed whether the airplane flies or not. The advantage is that once those fixed expenses are managed, the hourly cost of ownership can become lower than chartering, especially for high-utilization flyers.

Charter, on the other hand, comes with no long-term financial commitment. You pay only when you need to fly. The hourly rate is higher, but it includes everything such as fuel, crew, maintenance, and insurance, making it a predictable, one-line cost per trip. For travelers whose flight hours vary from month to month or season to season, this flexibility often outweighs the higher hourly rate.

If you fly often, owning may eventually reduce your overall cost per hour. But if your schedule is unpredictable or business travel is intermittent, chartering nearly always provides better value.

Control and Flexibility

Ownership means complete control. Your aircraft is available whenever you need it, ready to depart on your schedule. You can tailor the cabin design, technology, and onboard experience to your taste and maintain the same crew and configuration every flight.

Charter focuses on variety and ease. You can choose the right aircraft for each mission, light jets for short hops, midsize for regional routes, or large cabin aircraft for international trips. There’s no downtime, no maintenance planning, and no fixed expenses when you’re not flying. For most travelers, that simplicity is the main appeal.

If you fly frequently and want guaranteed availability and familiarity, ownership wins. If you value flexibility and variety, chartering gives you more freedom without the burden of management.

Flight Frequency

In practical terms, the number of hours you fly each year often dictates the right choice. Travelers logging fewer than fifty hours annually tend to benefit from on-demand charter. Those flying closer to one hundred hours often explore jet cards or memberships for more predictable pricing. Between one hundred and three hundred hours, fractional ownership can make sense. Beyond that threshold, full ownership usually provides the greatest efficiency and control.

Tax and Depreciation

For business owners, aircraft ownership can offer substantial tax advantages. Under Section 168(k) of the U.S. tax code, qualifying aircraft may be eligible for one hundred percent bonus depreciation in the first year if used primarily for business purposes. This allows owners to offset a large portion of the purchase price against taxable income.

Charter users, by contrast, can generally only deduct travel expenses related directly to business use. The tax difference between owning and chartering can be significant, so it’s essential to consult an aviation-focused CPA before making any purchase. The way the ownership entity is structured will determine eligibility for depreciation and deductions.

Lifestyle and Brand

Aircraft ownership is often as much about image and convenience as it is about travel. For many executives and business owners, it represents control, privacy, and reliability, values that reinforce credibility in front of clients and partners.

Charter delivers a similar luxury experience with far less responsibility. You still arrive in comfort, on your schedule, without worrying about maintenance or crew logistics. For entrepreneurs or families who fly occasionally, it’s often the smarter, cleaner way to access private aviation without the long-term financial commitment.

Hybrid Options

More flyers today are blending the two models. Fractional ownership programs like PennShare offer predictable costs, equity participation, and access to professionally managed aircraft without taking on full ownership. Leaseback programs can offset expenses by generating charter revenue when your plane isn’t in use. And jet card memberships provide guaranteed availability at fixed hourly rates, ideal for those who want consistency without full ownership responsibilities.

Final Approach

In the end, the right path depends on your flying habits, your business needs, and your financial goals. If you’re traveling frequently and want full control, ownership offers unmatched convenience and long-term value. If you prefer flexibility, lower commitment, and minimal management, chartering remains the most efficient choice.

At Penn Jets, our goal is to help clients calculate their true cost per flight hour, factoring in usage, depreciation, and potential revenue opportunities, so every decision is backed by accurate numbers. We can give you a clear understanding of what private aviation really costs, and btw, the answer is not time.

Ownership gives you control over scheduling, customization, and management, and with the right consulting and management team, it can also provide meaningful tax advantages. Without the right support, your new aircraft can quickly start controlling you instead of the other way around. Both Part 91 (private use) and Part 135 (charter) ownership come with fixed costs including maintenance, crew, insurance, hangar space, and management. The difference lies in their purpose and level of FAA regulatory compliance.

Under Part 135, an aircraft can legally generate charter revenue when operated in full compliance with FAA rules, standards, and oversight. Under Part 91, the operator is limited to private use only, meaning the aircraft cannot carry paying charter clientele. Both structures may still qualify for significant tax benefits, including potential bonus depreciation of up to 100 percent in the first year of ownership. To qualify, the aircraft must generally be used at least 50 percent for business purposes and meet individual financial and tax requirements.

Charter allows you to pay only when you fly. It’s flexible, straightforward, and commitment-free. You can choose aircraft types based on each trip and avoid the long-term responsibilities of ownership, a clean getaway for many travelers.

Cost Overview

When deciding between owning or chartering, the first factor that comes into play is cost. Ownership requires a significant upfront investment, anywhere from around one million dollars for a light jet to well over seventy million for a large cabin aircraft. Fractional ownership programs typically start between two hundred thousand and two million dollars depending on the share size and aircraft type.

Beyond the purchase, owners take on ongoing expenses: fuel, maintenance, insurance, hangar fees, crew salaries, and management oversight. These costs are fixed whether the airplane flies or not. The advantage is that once those fixed expenses are managed, the hourly cost of ownership can become lower than chartering, especially for high-utilization flyers.

Charter, on the other hand, comes with no long-term financial commitment. You pay only when you need to fly. The hourly rate is higher, but it includes everything such as fuel, crew, maintenance, and insurance, making it a predictable, one-line cost per trip. For travelers whose flight hours vary from month to month or season to season, this flexibility often outweighs the higher hourly rate.

If you fly often, owning may eventually reduce your overall cost per hour. But if your schedule is unpredictable or business travel is intermittent, chartering nearly always provides better value.

Control and Flexibility

Ownership means complete control. Your aircraft is available whenever you need it, ready to depart on your schedule. You can tailor the cabin design, technology, and onboard experience to your taste and maintain the same crew and configuration every flight.

Charter focuses on variety and ease. You can choose the right aircraft for each mission, light jets for short hops, midsize for regional routes, or large cabin aircraft for international trips. There’s no downtime, no maintenance planning, and no fixed expenses when you’re not flying. For most travelers, that simplicity is the main appeal.

If you fly frequently and want guaranteed availability and familiarity, ownership wins. If you value flexibility and variety, chartering gives you more freedom without the burden of management.

Flight Frequency

In practical terms, the number of hours you fly each year often dictates the right choice. Travelers logging fewer than fifty hours annually tend to benefit from on-demand charter. Those flying closer to one hundred hours often explore jet cards or memberships for more predictable pricing. Between one hundred and three hundred hours, fractional ownership can make sense. Beyond that threshold, full ownership usually provides the greatest efficiency and control.

Tax and Depreciation

For business owners, aircraft ownership can offer substantial tax advantages. Under Section 168(k) of the U.S. tax code, qualifying aircraft may be eligible for one hundred percent bonus depreciation in the first year if used primarily for business purposes. This allows owners to offset a large portion of the purchase price against taxable income.

Charter users, by contrast, can generally only deduct travel expenses related directly to business use. The tax difference between owning and chartering can be significant, so it’s essential to consult an aviation-focused CPA before making any purchase. The way the ownership entity is structured will determine eligibility for depreciation and deductions.

Lifestyle and Brand

Aircraft ownership is often as much about image and convenience as it is about travel. For many executives and business owners, it represents control, privacy, and reliability, values that reinforce credibility in front of clients and partners.

Charter delivers a similar luxury experience with far less responsibility. You still arrive in comfort, on your schedule, without worrying about maintenance or crew logistics. For entrepreneurs or families who fly occasionally, it’s often the smarter, cleaner way to access private aviation without the long-term financial commitment.

Hybrid Options

More flyers today are blending the two models. Fractional ownership programs like PennShare offer predictable costs, equity participation, and access to professionally managed aircraft without taking on full ownership. Leaseback programs can offset expenses by generating charter revenue when your plane isn’t in use. And jet card memberships provide guaranteed availability at fixed hourly rates, ideal for those who want consistency without full ownership responsibilities.

Final Approach

In the end, the right path depends on your flying habits, your business needs, and your financial goals. If you’re traveling frequently and want full control, ownership offers unmatched convenience and long-term value. If you prefer flexibility, lower commitment, and minimal management, chartering remains the most efficient choice.

At Penn Jets, our goal is to help clients calculate their true cost per flight hour, factoring in usage, depreciation, and potential revenue opportunities, so every decision is backed by accurate numbers. We can give you a clear understanding of what private aviation really costs, and btw, the answer is not time.

body.title: Canada’s Proposed 100% Aircraft Expensing: Could It Accelerate the Aircraft Replacement Cycle?
body.content:
Penn Jets was recently approached by a prospective client considering selling an existing aircraft and replacing it with a Dassault Falcon 900B. The conversation went quiet, in part because of current trade complexities. On September 15, 2026, Canada announced a proposal that made me think about that transaction again.

What Canada Is Proposing

Under the proposed Productivity Mega Deduction, a broad range of depreciable property acquired on or after September 15, 2026, including aircraft, would qualify for permanent immediate expensing. Instead of recovering an aircraft's cost gradually through the Capital Cost Allowance system, a qualifying taxpayer could deduct the full eligible amount in the year the aircraft becomes available for use.

To be clear, Canada is not changing an aircraft depreciation rate from 15% to 100%. The earlier Productivity Super-Deduction covered assets representing about 15% of capital investment. The Mega Deduction expands that to roughly two-thirds, now including aircraft.

It follows Canada's November 2025 repeal of its luxury tax on aircraft over $100,000. In less than a year, Canadian policy has moved from a luxury tax to a full first-year write-off.

Pre-Owned Aircraft Qualify

Used aircraft may qualify if neither the buyer nor a related party previously owned it and it was not transferred on a tax-deferred rollover basis. That opens the benefit to the U.S. pre-owned market.

Eligibility will depend on the final legislation and the buyer's circumstances. For individuals and partnerships with individual members, the draft rules limit the deduction to income from the business using the aircraft, and it cannot create or increase a loss.

Toronto and the Northeast

Toronto to New York, Boston and Philadelphia are short missions for midsize aircraft like the Citation Latitude, Challenger 350 and Praetor 500. Large-cabin aircraft like the Falcon 900 series fly the same routes while adding intercontinental range. U.S. buyers pursue the same aircraft.

If even some Canadian owners accelerate replacement, they enter the same pre-owned inventory. Once a buyer applies requirements for model, year, engine program and maintenance status, only a handful of comparable aircraft may be for sale. Any effect on values will likely show up first within individual models.

The Bombardier Question

On September 7, President Trump threatened to block Bombardier sales in the United States unless production moves to America, following a January threat to decertify Canadian-built aircraft. Implementation remains uncertain.

Canada's draft rules require certain passenger vehicles to be assembled in Canada but do not appear to impose a similar requirement on aircraft. Some Canadian demand could therefore flow toward U.S.-built Citations and Gulfstreams, French-built Falcons, Brazilian-built Embraers and pre-owned Bombardiers already on the U.S. market.

Canada has also imposed retaliatory tariffs on U.S. goods, so buyers should confirm whether any countermeasures affect a U.S.-sourced aircraft. Cross-border deals should involve Canadian tax advisors and aviation counsel alongside the broker, escrow and title professionals.

What Owners Should Consider

  • Eligibility under final legislation

  • Ownership structure and business use

  • Available-for-use timing

  • Current aircraft value and upcoming maintenance

  • Registration, import and tariffs

  • Financing and cash flow

The deduction should support a sensible acquisition, not turn the wrong aircraft into the right one.

Final Approach

For Canadian owners contemplating an upgrade, September 15, 2026 could become an important acquisition-date threshold. For American sellers, the question is whether some of that investment moves south. The transaction that crossed our desk went quiet, but the economics behind deals like it have become considerably more interesting.

Joseph Pennella
Penn Jets LLC

Sources: Department of Finance Canada, Sept. 15, 2026; Aviation International News, Sept. 18, 2026 and Nov. 6, 2025; Associated Press, Sept. 8, 2026.

body.title: Q3 2026: The Quarter Where the Paperwork Started to Matter
body.content:
Business aviation closes the third quarter with an unusual split. People are flying more. They are buying less. And for the first time in a while, the reason has less to do with the aircraft and more with where it was built and who is buying it.

Flying Up, Trading Down

Global business aviation flight activity rose 5.6% year over year in July, and North American activity climbed 4.3%, with fractional operators up 10% and Part 135 charter also gaining. Europe posted its first yearly decline in fourteen months. Global Business Aviation Flight Activity Surges 5.6 Percent in July 2026 – Aviation News +2

Transactions told a different story. Pre-owned whole-aircraft transactions totaled 1,115 in the first half, down 10.8% from the same period in 2025. Much of that gap is an echo: the tariff announcements of early 2025 pulled a large number of deals forward, and demand itself was largely unaffected. JetnetJetnet

Utilization is not the problem. Transaction friction is. Three events in Q3 explain most of it.

July 10: The Tariff That Was Held in Reserve

The administration ordered 180 days of talks rather than immediate Section 232 tariffs on commercial aircraft, jet engines and parts, sparing a sector with a $75 billion trade surplus while keeping the duties available. Brussels separately extended its suspension of retaliatory duties on American aircraft and parts, keeping roughly $4 billion in potential European retaliation off the table. PeacocktariffconsultingPeacocktariffconsulting

For anyone planning a cross-border transaction, this is the date to circle. The talks window runs into early January. A deal structured now under one set of assumptions may close under another.

August 21: U.S.–Canada Talks Collapse

Trade negotiations between the two countries broke down on August 21, followed by tariffs and threats, with Canada retaliating with tariffs on roughly $20 billion of U.S. goods. ClickOrlando

North America is a single aircraft market in practice. Toronto and the northeastern U.S. trade aircraft constantly. When the trade relationship gets complicated, so does every transaction that crosses the border.

September 7: Bombardier

The President posted that Bombardier can no longer sell in the United States unless it manufactures there. Bombardier responded that many components, including the wings, are built in the U.S., and that its supply chain includes about 2,800 American companies across 47 states. The threat would affect large fractional buyers, including NetJets, one of Bombardier's biggest customers. Trump threatens to block Canada’s Bombardier sales unless planes made in US | Donald Trump News | Al Jazeera +2

It was not the first such threat this year. In January, the President threatened to decertify Bombardier's large-cabin jets and all aircraft made in Canada, and to impose 50% tariffs on new planes. Nothing has been implemented. That may be the point worth making: the threat itself changes buyer behavior without a single rule being written. Al Jazeera

September 15: Canada Moves the Other Way

Canada announced its Productivity Mega Deduction, allowing businesses to immediately deduct 100% of the cost of a much broader range of investments. The measure raises covered assets from roughly 15% to more than 65%, and aircraft are explicitly on the list. Used property can qualify, provided neither the buyer nor a related party previously owned it and it was not acquired on a tax-deferred rollover. Productivity Mega Deduction Lowers Canada’s Investment Tax Rate +2

It follows Canada's repeal of its aircraft luxury tax in November 2025. Within a year, Canadian policy moved from taxing business aircraft to writing them off in full. We covered the implications for the U.S. pre-owned market separately.

What Actually Changed This Quarter

Country of manufacture, import history and ownership structure are now transaction variables, not footnotes. A buyer can be right about the airplane and still be surprised at closing.

Three practical consequences:

Diligence starts earlier. Export history, import structure and country of origin belong in the first conversation, not the week before closing.

Timing has a cost. With a tariff decision pending and a Canadian incentive dated to September 15, the calendar now carries real dollars.

The team is larger. Customs and tax counsel now sit alongside the broker, escrow and title on cross-border deals.

On the operating side, the same quarter's flight-activity numbers argue that demand is intact. Owners are using aircraft heavily even while deciding to wait on transactions, which is usually a sign of deferred activity rather than lost activity.

Looking to Q4

Watch the tariff talks window, the Canadian legislation as it moves from proposal to enacted law, and whether the fourth quarter delivers the transaction volume the first half deferred. Argus forecast North American flight activity to rise 3.5% year over year in the second half. Aviationnews

The aircraft market has absorbed worse. But Q3 was the quarter that made clear that in 2026, how a deal is structured matters as much as what is being bought.

Joseph Pennella
Penn Jets LLC

Market commentary only. Not tax, legal or investment advice.

body.title: The Largest Managed Fleet in the World Just Closed. What It Means for Owners.
body.content:
On October 1, Solairus Aviation closed its acquisition of Clay Lacy Aviation's aircraft management and charter divisions. The combined company manages more than 500 business aircraft, with roughly 200 on its Part 135 certificate.

That makes it the largest managed fleet in the world, and the largest transaction of its kind our segment has seen.

What Actually Changed Hands

Solairus managed about 360 aircraft from more than 100 bases across North America. Clay Lacy managed roughly 140, with a portfolio its website valued above $3 billion.

Only the management and charter divisions moved. Clay Lacy retains its FBOs, maintenance operations and real estate, and has said it will focus on growing a nationwide FBO network supported by maintenance and AOG capability.

Neither company owns the aircraft. They manage them for owners, which is why this transaction is unusual: the asset being acquired is a book of relationships, and those relationships can decline to come along.

More than 135 Clay Lacy owners have confirmed they are moving to Solairus. The transition runs in two tranches, the first on October 1 and the second on November 1.

Why Scale Is Happening Now

Management is an unusually fragmented business. Most aircraft management companies operate fewer than five aircraft. Real economies of scale begin somewhere past 100 or 250 aircraft, in fuel purchasing, insurance, parts, training and crew pipelines.

Rising operating costs have made that math harder to ignore. Larger operators can negotiate better and absorb cost increases that a five-aircraft manager simply passes through to owners.

Capital has noticed. Solairus has been owned since 2022 by Ancient, the firm founded by Alexander Klabin, which also owns the superyacht brokerage Burgess and Sotheby's Financial. That portfolio tells you how this asset class is being viewed: aircraft management sits alongside yachts and art lending as a business built on servicing significant private wealth.

What Owners Should Expect

If your aircraft is managed by either company, the practical questions are specific:

Who is your actual point of contact next month? Integration means people change seats. The named individual who knows your aircraft and your travel patterns matters more than the logo on the invoice.

What happens to your charter revenue? Roughly 200 aircraft on one certificate means a larger pool competing for the same trips. Scale can mean more charter demand routed to your aircraft, or more aircraft competing for the trips you used to get. Ask how trip assignment works.

Does your management agreement transfer unchanged? Rates, revenue splits, maintenance authority and termination provisions are worth rereading now, not at renewal.

Will your crew stay? Crew retention through an integration is the single best predictor of whether owners notice the change.

For everyone else, there's a quieter consequence. Salespeople from competing management companies have already begun calling Clay Lacy owners. Any transition creates an opening, and owners who were already lukewarm about their arrangement will hear from alternatives.

The Broader Pattern

This is consolidation reaching a part of the industry that resisted it for a long time. Fractional providers consolidated years ago. Charter brokers have been consolidating steadily. FBO networks went through it twice.

Management was the holdout, because the business is local, relationship-driven and hard to scale without losing the personal service owners pay for. Both companies have emphasized that high-touch service is what they intend to preserve. Whether a 500-aircraft fleet can feel like a 40-aircraft fleet is the real question, and the answer will take a year to see.

What won't change is the underlying choice facing owners. Management is not a commodity. The right structure depends on how much you fly, whether you want charter revenue, how much operational control you want to retain and how much you value having someone who answers the phone at 11pm on a Sunday.

Bigger buys better. Smaller sometimes answers faster. Both can be the right answer, depending on the owner.

Our View

As both a broker and a partner in a Part 135 operation, we watch these transactions closely. Scale changes the economics of operating an aircraft, and the economics of operating an aircraft change what an aircraft is worth to own.

If you are evaluating management options, or reconsidering an arrangement because of this transition, we are happy to walk through the structures with you.

Joseph Pennella
Penn Jets LLC

Solairus managed about 360 aircraft from more than 100 bases across North America. Clay Lacy managed roughly 140, with a portfolio its website valued above $3 billion.

Only the management and charter divisions moved. Clay Lacy retains its FBOs, maintenance operations and real estate, and has said it will focus on growing a nationwide FBO network supported by maintenance and AOG capability.

Neither company owns the aircraft. They manage them for owners, which is why this transaction is unusual: the asset being acquired is a book of relationships, and those relationships can decline to come along.

More than 135 Clay Lacy owners have confirmed they are moving to Solairus. The transition runs in two tranches, the first on October 1 and the second on November 1.

Why Scale Is Happening Now

Management is an unusually fragmented business. Most aircraft management companies operate fewer than five aircraft. Real economies of scale begin somewhere past 100 or 250 aircraft, in fuel purchasing, insurance, parts, training and crew pipelines.

Rising operating costs have made that math harder to ignore. Larger operators can negotiate better and absorb cost increases that a five-aircraft manager simply passes through to owners.

Capital has noticed. Solairus has been owned since 2022 by Ancient, the firm founded by Alexander Klabin, which also owns the superyacht brokerage Burgess and Sotheby's Financial. That portfolio tells you how this asset class is being viewed: aircraft management sits alongside yachts and art lending as a business built on servicing significant private wealth.

What Owners Should Expect

If your aircraft is managed by either company, the practical questions are specific:

Who is your actual point of contact next month? Integration means people change seats. The named individual who knows your aircraft and your travel patterns matters more than the logo on the invoice.

What happens to your charter revenue? Roughly 200 aircraft on one certificate means a larger pool competing for the same trips. Scale can mean more charter demand routed to your aircraft, or more aircraft competing for the trips you used to get. Ask how trip assignment works.

Does your management agreement transfer unchanged? Rates, revenue splits, maintenance authority and termination provisions are worth rereading now, not at renewal.

Will your crew stay? Crew retention through an integration is the single best predictor of whether owners notice the change.

For everyone else, there's a quieter consequence. Salespeople from competing management companies have already begun calling Clay Lacy owners. Any transition creates an opening, and owners who were already lukewarm about their arrangement will hear from alternatives.

The Broader Pattern

This is consolidation reaching a part of the industry that resisted it for a long time. Fractional providers consolidated years ago. Charter brokers have been consolidating steadily. FBO networks went through it twice.

Management was the holdout, because the business is local, relationship-driven and hard to scale without losing the personal service owners pay for. Both companies have emphasized that high-touch service is what they intend to preserve. Whether a 500-aircraft fleet can feel like a 40-aircraft fleet is the real question, and the answer will take a year to see.

What won't change is the underlying choice facing owners. Management is not a commodity. The right structure depends on how much you fly, whether you want charter revenue, how much operational control you want to retain and how much you value having someone who answers the phone at 11pm on a Sunday.

Bigger buys better. Smaller sometimes answers faster. Both can be the right answer, depending on the owner.

Our View

As both a broker and a partner in a Part 135 operation, we watch these transactions closely. Scale changes the economics of operating an aircraft, and the economics of operating an aircraft change what an aircraft is worth to own.

If you are evaluating management options, or reconsidering an arrangement because of this transition, we are happy to walk through the structures with you.

body.title: Charter Demand Is Up 27%. Flying Isn’t
body.content:
A Charter Request Is Not a Charter Flight

U.S. charter demand rose 27% between October 2025 and last month, according to Avinode.

That number is going to get quoted a lot. It is worth knowing what it measures.

Avinode is a marketplace where brokers search for aircraft and operators quote back. What it counts as demand is trip requests submitted on the platform.

A request is not a flight. It is someone asking.

Avinode Says So Themselves

This is not my inference. It is in the same article.

Harry Clarke, Avinode’s director of commercial development, says the number of actual departures is “pretty flat in the U.S. year over year.” He goes further: “The market is flat overall right now.”

Requests up 27%. Departures flat. Both from the same platform, in the same report.

Why the Two Numbers Diverge

Clarke gives the reason directly. He describes a “very competitive environment,” evidenced by a record number of U.S.-based charter brokers using the platform.

If three brokers quote the same trip, the platform records three requests and one airplane leaves the ground.

More brokers joining a marketplace raises request volume whether or not a single additional passenger flies. The marketplace gets busier. The market does not get bigger.

Clarke calls the last few years a “calmer situation, with more people trying to be involved in facilitating this sort of travel.” That is a polite description of a crowded intermediary layer, and it is the most useful thing in the report.

What Flying Actually Looks Like

For context, JETNET and WINGX data presented at the JIQ fireside chat on September 30 put global Part 135 charter departures up 4.3% this year, with fractional up 9.9% and owner-flown Part 91 up 0.6%.

That is a global figure. Clarke is speaking about the U.S. specifically, where WingX data suggests roughly two-thirds of all charter flights take place.

Read together: charter flying is growing modestly worldwide, and in the U.S. it is close to flat. Neither picture resembles 27%.

The Part That Should Concern Owners

Here is what I would not skip past.

Avinode expects hourly charter rates to hit a record high through the remainder of 2026, driven by holiday demand and rising fuel costs.

Flat departures. Record rates.

If you own an aircraft on a Part 135 certificate, that combination deserves attention. Higher rates do not automatically mean higher revenue when the number of trips is not growing and the broker count is. It means the same volume of flying is being repriced, and more intermediaries are competing to place it.

We wrote earlier this month about Jet A reaching a six-month high, up 32.7% since January. Clarke names fuel as one of the two drivers of those record rates. That is the cost showing up on the other side of the invoice.

If You Are Building a Charter Revenue Projection

Ask which number it rests on.

A 27% rise in requests does not tell you how many revenue hours you will fly next year. Flat departures do.

Build the projection off marketplace demand figures and you will overestimate utilization and underestimate what the aircraft actually costs you to own. The spreadsheet looks reasonable in January. The invoices disagree by June.

Final Approach

Avinode publishes what its platform records, and their own executive was careful to say the market is flat. The caution is in the reporting. It is just below the headline.

Twenty-seven percent is a real number. It answers a different question than most readers will assume: not how many people are flying, but how many people are asking on behalf of them.

For a market heading into its peak season with record rates and flat volume, that distinction is worth getting right.

Joseph Pennella
Penn Jets LLC

body.title: 617 Aircraft, 21 for Sale: Inside the G550 Market
body.content:
617 Aircraft, 21 for Sale

I went looking for a late-model G550 for a client.

Here is what the market actually had.

Per JETNET, there are 617 G550s in operation. Twenty-one are for sale. That is 3.4% of the fleet.

Across business aviation as a whole, about 6.6% of aircraft are listed. Nine to ten percent is what usually makes a buyer’s market.

So the G550 is sitting at roughly half the market-wide rate.

Then I narrowed to 2015 and newer. That is 128 airframes. Two were on the market, and one of those was in for maintenance.

One airplane.

Supply Cannot Grow

The number nobody looks at is production. It is zero. Gulfstream Aerospace ended commercial production and delivered its final commercial G550 on June 30, 2021, wrapping up an 18-year manufacturing run that began in 2003.

The Spread Is the Real Story

JETNET puts absorption at 3.9 months. If nothing new were listed, current inventory clears in under four months.

But look at days on market. The low is 2 days. The high is 994. The average is 106.

One aircraft sold in two days. Another has been listed for almost three years.

That is not a tight market. That is a bifurcated one.

The right airplane, priced right, is gone in days. The wrong one sits for years at a number nobody will pay.

There is no average G550 for sale. The average is useless to a buyer.

Why 596 Owners Are Not Selling

The number I keep coming back to is 596.

That is how many owners are not in the market to sell.

At the JIQ fireside chat last month, Richard Koe showed owner-flown Part 91 activity up just 0.6% this year. Fractional was up 9.9%. Charter was up 4.3%.

Most people read flat Part 91 as ownership losing ground.

I read it differently.

A corporate flight department is not a revenue asset. It is executive logistics. The aircraft exists so a few people can be somewhere on short notice.

That requirement does not care what the airplane is worth.

An owner running a G550 on Part 91 is not holding an underperforming asset. They are holding a capability. There is no price that makes the logistics problem go away.

Which usually means there is no price that triggers a sale.

What This Means If You Are Buying

Know what you actually need before you commit to a spec. Every requirement you add cuts into a pool that starts at 21 worldwide.

Be ready to move. A two-day low on days-on-market means the good ones are gone before a slow buyer finishes thinking.

Read the long listings correctly. An airplane at 994 days is not a bargain waiting to happen. It is a pricing, records or specification problem, and it becomes your problem on resale.

Work off-market. Twenty of the 21 listings are on exclusive. The published inventory is not the real market. The real market is a conversation with an owner who was not planning to sell.

Final Approach

Transactions across business aviation were down in the first half of this year. That is the headline.

It is not what a buyer experiences.

If you want this specific airplane, you are not in a soft market. You are in a market with one airplane for you in it, if you're lucky.

Twenty-one for sale. Seventeen in the United States. One that fit the requirement.

That is the market.

Joseph Pennella
Penn Jets LLC

body.content:
Jet A at a Six-Month High: What It Actually Costs

Jet A hit a six-month high in September. The number worth knowing isn’t the monthly move. It’s that full-service Jet A is up 32.7% since January.

Per iFlightPlanner’s monthly survey of 3,370 FBOs and fuel providers, the national average reached $8.36 a gallon, up 4.9% from August. The Eastern region fared worst, at $8.69 and up 7.0% — the largest monthly increase in the Lower 48. For anyone based between Teterboro and Boston, that is your ramp.

What it costs in practice: by our arithmetic, a midsize jet burning roughly 200 gallons an hour pays about $78 more per flight hour than it did in August. At 300 hours a year, that’s $23,000. Measured from January instead, the same airplane is carrying six figures more in annual fuel.

Two caveats worth stating plainly. Full-service retail is the posted price, not what most operators actually pay — contract fuel and volume programs land well below it. And fuel is one line in an operating budget, not the whole thing.

But it moves faster than the others, and it moves first. Maintenance reserves and crew costs are negotiated annually. Fuel reprices every month, and right now it is repricing in one direction.

The reported driver is the continuing war in Iran and the supply constraint that comes with it. That is not something an owner can plan around, which is the point. It belongs in the category of costs you budget conservatively rather than forecast precisely.

For charter buyers, expect fuel surcharges to follow. For owners weighing utilization, this is the kind of input that quietly changes the math on flying versus chartering out. And for anyone building a 2027 operating budget this quarter, a January baseline is now 33% stale.

Joseph Pennella
Penn Jets LLC
